title: THE FAKE VIDEO CALL THAT STOLE $400 MILLION

click the link. And
there they are, waiting in the lobby.
Same face. Same room.
Then a message pops up. We can't hear you.
Click here to fix it. You click.
Because your friend was never there. That was
a recording. And
the FBI says this trick has stolen more than
four hundred million dollars.
It's called FaceStealer.
On November twelfth, the FBI and the Justice Department went public.
They say North Korean state hackers have run this scheme for the last
eighteen months. And
it starts with a webcam.
Meet Victim A. The hackers already own their computer. They've
scanned it for crypto wallets and seed phrases. They've
locked them out of their Telegram account. And while Victim A waited for a video chat to start, the hackers
secretly recorded their webcam.
Now the hackers become Victim A. They
message every contact, from the real account. Let's
catch up. Let's discuss collaboration. Let's talk about investment opportunities. And
because they can read the chat history, the messages to high- value targets are tailored to past conversations.
Say yes, and a calendar invite arrives. Without a meeting link. The link only comes
shortly before the call, so the hackers expose their servers as little as possible. And
it isn't Zoom, or Teams. It's a look- alike address, registered by the hackers, that opens
a copycat meeting room, designed to be indistinguishable from the real thing. You click. You
wait in the lobby. You're admitted. And the hackers
press play on Victim A's stored webcam video. Often with
extra videos, so the room looks full of people you know.
After a short delay, a message from your friend. They say there's an audio problem, and nobody can hear you. The
fake participants add pressure. It seems like only you are broken. So your friend
guides you through the fix. Click an update. Run a script. Or copy and paste code into your terminal.
That's the infection. The malware installs a
cookie harvester, keyloggers, screen capturers, and a backdoor. And
the moment you clicked that first link, they'd already started recording your webcam.
You've become the next Victim A. With every victim, and every stolen contact list, the FBI says the pool of targets grows
exponentially. And the hackers are
patient. In several cases, the theft came months, even more than a year, after the first compromise. They copied seed phrases,
watched the wallet balances, and waited for the money to grow.
Here's what the FBI seized. The cloud servers behind the scheme. And more than
nine hundred webcam videos of real victims.
So where's the A I? The
FBI says the hackers have started using what it calls super intelligence to make
deepfake videos of famous names in crypto, built from public photos and videos. The
quality only needs to be good enough to pass as a webcam. But here's
the twist. The FBI says the scheme still overwhelmingly relies on genuine, stolen video. They
didn't need a deepfake. Your face was enough. It gets
worse. Earlier this year, hackers used the same trick on
a maintainer of a major open- source JavaScript library. A
fake Teams call, with several participants, including someone he recognised. He
followed the fix. Then the hackers used his access to create
malicious dependencies, which would have downloaded alongside the real library. A library with
tens of millions of downloads a week.
Only quick detection stopped it. The FBI
attributes all of this to North Korean state- sponsored hackers, known
as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff, A P T thirty- eight, and Stardust Chollima. The
Justice Department says North Korea's government uses crypto theft to
bankroll its weapons programme. The
same day, the Justice Department described a separate case. On or about
October twenty- ninth, it says North Korean military hackers, called
TraderTraitor by the FBI, stole more than
six billion dollars from the exchange Binance. It's
a different attack, and the Justice Department calls it separate from FaceStealer. Authorities have
frozen more than two point seven billion dollars, and got
court approval to seize or restrain over one point two billion. So how do
you avoid becoming the next victim?
One. Join with the official app and an invite code, not a link.
Two. Keep your webcam off until you can see and hear the person who invited you.
Three. Never run a script, or paste code, to fix a meeting.
Four. Confirm the call on a different channel from the one they used. And
five. Turn on multi- factor authentication for Telegram, Slack and WhatsApp, and
keep large crypto balances on a separate hardware ledger, with no recovery phrases on your devices.
If you think you've been hit, move your funds to a new wallet, on a clean device.
Warn your contacts, because they're the next targets. And
report it at I C three dot gov, with the keyword FaceStealer. Here's what
to remember. A familiar face on a screen is no longer proof.
Before you click join, ask yourself: is this person really here? If this helped,
subscribe, and send it to someone in crypto or open source.
Because the next call might not be a friend.
